extracted.intended_audience: general readers and performers interested in music hall history and performance
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and descriptive criteria for creating, programming, or evaluating music-hall/variety acts (Victorian–Edwardian British tradition) including comic performers, song material, impersonation, mime, speciality acts, and audience interaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Typical comedian presentation (persona and staging)
rubrics_metrics.description: The typical music hall comedian was a man or woman, usually dressed in character to suit the subject of the song, or sometimes attired in absurd and eccentric style. Until well into the twentieth century, the acts were essentially vocal, with songs telling a story, accompanied by a minimum of patter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a clear stage persona or costume that matches the song's subject; prioritize strong, story-telling vocal numbers; keep spoken patter minimal and functional. Examples: character-driven performers like Marie Lloyd, Harry Champion, Vesta Victoria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Song material: narrative, topicality, and catchy choruses
rubrics_metrics.description: Songs typically told a story and could be topical or parodic (e.g., 'topical vocalist' Fred Albert). Many music-hall hits featured memorable choruses and easily sung refrains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write songs that communicate a simple narrative or joke, include a strong chorus to encourage audience singalongs, and consider topical or parodic references to increase immediate appeal. Examples: 'The Lambeth Walk', 'Any Old Iron', 'Waiting at the Church'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-specific thematic conventions (lion comiques)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lion comiques: essentially, men dressed as 'toffs', who sang songs about drinking champagne, going to the races, going to the ball, womanising and gambling, and living the life of an aristocrat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If working in a subgenre (e.g., lion comique), adhere to its thematic and visual tropes to meet audience expectations; use satire of upper‑class life and flamboyant costume to create character comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impersonation (male/female) as a device for comedy and commentary
rubrics_metrics.description: Male and female impersonators were common. Female impersonators were often in the style of a pantomime dame; some more sophisticated performers (e.g., Vesta Tilley, Ella Shields) used male impersonations to communicate real social commentary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use impersonation not only for caricature but as a means to comment on gender and society; tailor costuming and mannerisms to the impersonated role. Note: styles range from broad pantomime dame to nuanced social commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fred Karno/speechless sketch technique (mime and physicality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fred Karno developed a form of sketch comedy without dialogue in the 1890s. Karno's 'Speechless Comedians' trained performers to express each thought and attitude in mime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider non-verbal sketch work where physical mime, timing and visual gag structure convey the joke; train performers in mime/physical comedy. Examples: Karno's 'Mumming Birds' sketch and alumni Charlie Chaplin and Stan Laurel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Speciality acts and the value of variety/novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: Music hall bills included many kinds of 'speciality acts' ('spesh') — adagio (dance/juggling), aerial acts, animal acts, cycling acts, strongmen/strongwomen, drag artists, electric acts, escapologists, fire-eaters, juggling, magic, memory acts, mentalism, mime, impressionists, comic pianists, puppet and shadow-puppet acts, stilt walkers, trampolines, ventriloquists, Wild West/cowboy acts, wrestling and jujitsu exhibitions, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Program a diverse mix of novelty and spectacle alongside songs to maintain audience interest; speciality acts should offer visual surprise or technical feat. Use unusual/‘weird and wonderful’ acts to distinguish a bill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of bill: integrating vocal numbers with speciality turns
rubrics_metrics.description: The vocal content of music hall bills was, from the beginning, accompanied by many other kinds of act; acts were essentially vocal with a minimum of patter but supported by speciality turns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure a show so that story-songs and comic turns alternate with visually spectacular speciality acts to vary pace and keep audiences engaged; avoid long runs of the same format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Audience participation and communal elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Audience participation was common (e.g., on The Good Old Days audiences joined in singing, especially of choruses like 'Down at the Old Bull and Bush').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include singable refrains and moments for crowd engagement; encourage call-and-response or communal choruses, particularly at the close of a programme to leave a strong shared memory.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performer-authored and topical material
rubrics_metrics.description: Many performers wrote their own material and 'topical vocalists' (e.g., Fred Albert) created songs tied to contemporary life and news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage performers to write original material reflecting current events or local colour to increase immediacy and relevance; original authorship can enhance performer identity and distinctiveness.
